I will, however, try and answer from an Australians perspective. For Australia and New Zealand, I think the true roots of this'near-hero worship' of our soldiers, or'diggers' as they are called in Australia, came from World War I. More specifically, the battle of Gallipoli. Before this battle, the soldiers of both these nations had never quite taken part in a true, nation defining battle or war. And with the outbreak of World War I, Australia and New Zealand formed the ANZAC's, the Australian and New Zealand Army Corpse. This is particularly significant as it was the first time both the Australians and the New Zealander's fought together, side by side. The main role they served in the war was to capture the Ottoman post that sat there. This move was actually co-ordinated by the British, who were planning to use the post to stage an offensive on Constantinople. However the operation did not go to plan. The Ottoman forces dug themselves in, and managed to hold off the allied forces, leading to an eventual victory after 8 months of fighting. This battle for the ANZAC's, quite simply, was an absolute bloodbath. Because of the trench warfare style of war used in WWI, the ANZAC's were dug into the side of the hill and basically couldn't move forward. This lead to many attempted charges up over the hill and into the enemy trench line. However because of the well positioned Ottoman machine guns and trenches overlooking the ANZAC position, it meant that the ANZAC's stood no chance, and were mowed down time and time again. What came from this are the stories of great heroism surrounding these soldiers, who would run into open battle where almost certain death awaited them, and yet they continued to try again and again. The battle played an enormous role in forging the national identities of these two countries; these two small island nations on the other side of the world, fighting side by side, tooth and nail, for their countries and for their Queen. Their tremendous heroism is echoed every year on ANZAC day, where veterans of both countries parade in their cities, and remember the fallen.," "The Ancient Greek and Roman cultures seem to have taken military service as a sign of good moral character, and the fact that soldiers could be seen as selfless has often encouraged a view of them as heroes. For governments, it is also politically useful for soldiers to seem like the good guys, because they're doing what the government wants them too (so the government might look better, too). The armed forces themselves also encourage this sense of heroism, because it can help troops' morale and recruitment.

an invaluable resource for a company of all sizes to get advice from more experienced people in the field, or just at managing a company. It is not uncommon for executives of companies in the same field, but not directly competing, to sit on the board of a company. When getting started in such a cut throat world, someone always available to ask for advice or to simply yank your chain when you are about to go off the deep end can save the company. Technically, the founders start out as the board of the company, and as they seek out investors, the investors typically want a place on the board themselves, or the ability to name someone to the board. They do this so they can have some form of control in their sizable investment. They can even force a founder to step down from the CEO position in favor of someone with more experience. (This is not uncommon, as it is extraordinarily rare for someone to possess the skills to both successfully start a company and the skills to run it once it has grown.) It is also important to note that while a founder can be fired, heshe still retains any ownership they have in the company. Board members can get this voting power, because when you seek out investors, you typically give very large portions of the company to your investors in return for their investment. Hence the concept of a "valuation." This is getting into investing, but the short version is that when you ask an Angel Investor for 2 million, he may ask for 50 of your company because the company is only worth a total of 4 million. When seeking out a Venture Capital firm, a company like Spotify can ask for 400 million at a 4 billion valuation and only give away 10 of their company (and 10 of their votes). So, we'll say the owner is now at the point where the company is valued at 100 million, but their share has been diluted down to 10, thus they only get 10 of the vote. If all the board members vote to kick him out as the CEO, he's got to go, because he no longer controls the majority of the company. He still has a net worth of 10 million, they can't take that away, but now he is simply an owner of the company instead of an owner who happens to be the CEO. He still gets his 10 vote, and if he can convince a majority of the owners (in percentages) to vote him back in as CEO, he's right back on top.', "When Zuckerberg took the company private he owned only 28.2 of the company. The geometry of bicycles and motorcycles means that leaning them causes them to steer. Gyroscope effects are sometimes mentioned here too, but it has a lot to do with the shape of the tire. The edge is shorter, and therefore moving slower, than the center of the tire. When leaned, the center wants to cover more ground and "catch up" with the side of the tire. This causes the bike to turn. The turning of the bike makes it straighten up, due to a moving object's tendency to keep moving in a straight line (when turning, it leans to the outside of the curve). Once it straightens up, it stops turning. So you might notice a small deviation from a straight line but it's not going to continue turning. The correction is self-limiting and when you're moving these "corrections" are so quick and constant it just feels like a force or natural tendency for the bike to stay upright.','Minute Physics did a video about it. The gyroscopic effect is a common answer, but tests have been done to try and cancel out the gyroscopic effect of bikes and they are still fairly self-correcting. And the geometry is mentioned, but people have made very strangely shaped bikes that we can still make work like bikes with relative ease. It seems that each of the working theories on how bicyclesmotorcycles stay up has something to do with it, but there's still some mystery there.,A moving object will not fall over. feeding a magma chamber in the crust (which doesn't necessarily erupt too often). The Yellowstone hot spot feeds the magma chamber in the crust above for instance, though that hasn't erupted in well over half a million years. The other important point about hot spots is that they can occur anywhere within a tectonic plate. The vast majority of volcanism is associated with plate boundaries, as certain processes that occur there fuel eruptions. Hot spots are associated with mantle plumes, whose positions are not dictated by tectonic plates, and may originate from as far down as the boundary between mantle and (outer) core. With regards to ash, this is pyroclastic fire-broken material with a grain size of 2mm. Pyroclasts or tephra (interchangeable, they both refer to all sizes) are the fragments of rock and glass that are produced by more explosive volcanic eruptions, often also called tephra. Due to their small size, volcanic ash particles cool and solidify almost instantaneously upon eruption into the air. So what makes an eruption explosive? This is almost entirely down to the volatile content of a magma (chiefly water, but also carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and some other minor ones). Without this, any magma would erupt as an effusive one, in which molten rock would dribble down the flanks of a volcano or fissure at various speeds, or at best create a lava fountain a few metres high. The thing about volatiles like water is that in a magma chamber they are confined by the pressure of the overlying crust (they are usually 1-10km deep) and so they are dissolved within the magma, minding their own business. If some of the magma starts rising then the pressure will decrease as it nears the surface, volatiles will change phase to a gas (with a large volume expansion) and coalesce to form bubbles. If the magma ascent is rapid enough and the bubbles are forming vigorously, there comes a time when individual bubbles cannot be considered in isolation - they interact with one another, making the magma more like the foam on top of a beer than a simple fluid. In eruptions with a sudden release of a lot of pressure, this all happens extrmely quickly and the magma is literally torn into little fragments which we call ash if they are erupted at less than 2 mm diameter. That build up and sudden release of pressure doesn't happen explosively enough to form ash in all eruptions though. Stromboli, the lighthouse of the Mediterranean has a fairly high water content in its magma, but the frequency of eruption (every half an hour or so) prevents pressure building up, and the composition of the magma is thin enough to permit easy separation of bubbles from the melt. So we end up with bubbles, snaps and impressive lava fountains, though they are modest by a volcano's standards. Viscosity, or'thickness' of a magma is controlled by temperature (lower temp more viscous) and chemical composition (higher silica content more viscous). It just so happens that magmas higher in silica melt at lower temperatures, and so they form the most viscous ones. They also tend to produce the typical large conical volcano form of most people's imagination, which produces significant overburden on a magma chamber, and previous eruptions may leave behind some of the most firmly emplaced volcanic'plugs' or sealed conduits from magma chamber to surface. All of this means that magma which is high in silica, low in temp, high in volatile content, and having to overcome a large overpressure, will eventually do so in explosive fashion, creating large volumes of ash and other pyroclastic material. These are the most dangerous type of eruptions due to their immediacy, scale, and hazards for aircraft and local residents. Pyroclastic density currents are what happens when the eruption column collapses and rolls down the side of a volcano at hundreds of km per hour and many hundreds of deg C. This is what spelled instant death (and subsequent preservation) for the residents of Pompeii in 79 AD.,To quote the beginning of the [wiki article on Volcanic ash] (URL0) Volcanic ash consists of fragments of pulverized rock, minerals and volcanic glass, created during volcanic eruptions and measuring less than 2 mm (0.079 inches) in diameter.[1] The term volcanic ash is also often loosely used to refer to all explosive eruption products (correctly referred to as tephra), including particles larger than 2mm. Volcanic ash is formed during explosive volcanic eruptions when dissolved gases in magma expand and escape violently into the atmosphere. The force of the escaping gas shatters the magma and propels it into the atmosphere where it solidifies into fragments of volcanic rock and glass. Ash is also produced when magma comes into contact with water during phreatomagmatic eruptions, causing the water to explosively flash to steam leading to shattering of magma. Once in the air, ash is transported by wind up to thousands of kilometers away.
